Header:
Date: 2027-02-15
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Aurelius CTO), Sofia (Dir Infra), Liam (SRE), Meera (Security)

Summary (auto): quick deep dive on private VPC networking for Redwood Private deployment. Covered PrivateLink, NAT/egress, subnets, DNS, and runtime tradeoffs (KV cache, batching, quantization). Action items and follow-ups agreed.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood, this is priya and ethan our solutions eng team. how's everyone doing?
[00:05] Carlos: hey thanks, all good. excited to dig in — we've got a pretty strict network and security bar so wanted to run through the specifics.
[00:12] Priya: great, we'll run through architecture options first (PrivateLink/peering/transit), then runtime side — kv cache behavior, batching, quantization, and how those map to latency and throughput in a private deployment.
[00:20] Sofia: quick items from our side — we run in AWS us-east-1 with multiple accounts per environment, strict egress rules (only via approved proxies), and a desire to avoid public internet egress for inference traffic. we also have limited spare /16 ranges so IP usage matters.
[00:35] Ethan: noted. so high level, the two common patterns we see:
- PrivateLink (AWS NLB + interface endpoints) from customer VPC to redwood-managed endpoints in a partner VPC or across accounts — TLS stays internal, no internet egress for data plane.
- VPC peering / Transit Gateway with an L3 route — more hands-on networking and sometimes simpler IP routing but can be tricky cross-account and scales differently.
[00:55] Liam: peering sounds ok but transit gateway is expensive and we have multiple accounts. how does PrivateLink affect performance? any extra latency?
[01:04] Priya: PrivateLink adds ~1-3 ms typically on top of the baseline network RT. in our benchmarks for similar setups we saw 2.1 ms median overhead, depends on path and NLB. the bigger variables tend to be NAT/egress and DNS resolution if you have split-horizon.
[01:20] Meera: we require traffic to stay in our VPCs and be visible in VPC flow logs for audit. can PrivateLink preserve logs/auditability?
[01:27] Jordan: yes, you get flow logs on your interface endpoint and we provide request-level audit logs from the control plane (with PII redaction options). we'll share the SOC2 and logging docs.
[01:35] Carlos: what about IP addressing — you mentioned ENIs. how many IPs do we need per endpoint?
[01:40] Ethan: each interface endpoint consumes an ENI per AZ, and scale depends on number of concurrent connections. typical guidance: reserve /28 per AZ for endpoints + headroom. for heavy throughput we sometimes recommend NLB-backed PrivateLink with multiple subnets.
[02:00] Sofia: we have tight IP space; can we use NAT and egress proxies to multiplex?
[02:05] Priya: yes — egress via NAT or proxy is common. caveat: if you route through a proxy that does TLS-terminating you may change the TLS context and that affects mTLS and KMS key usage. for private deployments we recommend end-to-end TLS with mutual auth to preserve customer control.
[02:22] Liam: can redwood run inside our VPC (on-prem equivalent) — like a managed instance or agent?
[02:28] Jordan: Redwood Private runs with a customer-controlled data plane. we can deploy nodes into your VPC (or on-prem) with our control plane optionally out-of-band. that model avoids public egress. we also support an air-gapped on-prem bundle for highly regulated customers.
[02:42] Carlos: ok can you talk about latency sources in the runtime? specifically kv cache lookup, batching delays, and quantization tradeoffs.
[02:50] Priya: absolutely. kv cache: when we pin models with long-context workloads the KV cache reduces repeated compute by serving prefix context from memory; cache hits are in-memory operations and save tens to hundreds of ms depending on model size. but cache warmup is important — the first request has to populate the cache.
[03:10] Priya: batching introduces an intentional wait to aggregate tokens across concurrent requests; for low-latency SLOs we use small dynamic batches or single-request fast-paths. for throughput cost saving we allow larger batches — tradeoff is extra queuing latency. our recommendation: configure latency SLOs per route and let the runtime pick batching thresholds.
[03:30] Ethan: quantization reduces memory and kernel runtimes; going from fp16 to 4-bit can reduce per-token compute and memory by ~2-3x but you may see small quality diffs. for many prompt types we recommend 8-bit quantization first, run evals, then try 4-bit where acceptable. quantization interacts with kernel selection and sometimes affects KV cache footprint positively.
[03:55] Sofia: if we run in our VPC, how is telemetry/metrics shipped back to redwood console? we need logs retained in our account.
[04:03] Jordan: telemetry has two models: metrics-only aggregated telemetry to our control plane (no PII) and customer-controlled logs. for Private deployments we support shipping raw logs to your S3 or CloudWatch via a connector, or you can keep logs entirely in your account and we only get a thin health ping. we'll document the options.
[04:20] Carlos: about DNS — we operate split-horizon for internal services. how do we make sure our internal hostnames map to the right endpoints and avoid leaking to public DNS?
[04:28] Priya: we support private DNS zones and you can set up conditional forwarding to our VPC endpoint. best practice: create a private hosted zone (e.g., redwood-private.company.internal) and point records to ENIs or interface endpoint IPs. also we provide guidance for Route 53 resolver rules to forward to our resolver endpoints when needed.
[04:50] Liam: question on NAT bandwidth and socket limits — our infra sometimes hits ephemeral port exhaustion with large concurrent connections. how does redwood handle connection reuse?
[04:59] Ethan: we use HTTP/2 and connection pooling across clients to minimize new sockets; the client SDK uses long-lived connections and request multiplexing. still, if you terminate via a proxy/NAT with limited source ports, you need to ensure sufficient ephemeral port capacity or use NAT Gateway scaling. we can also recommend an internal ALB in front of a small proxy pool.
[05:20] Meera: KMS — we require customer-managed keys for data at rest encryption. is that supported?
[05:26] Jordan: yes; for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support envelope encryption. we'll send the KMS integration doc.
[05:33] Carlos: you mentioned fallbacks earlier — if a model variant is down or capacity is constrained, what's the behavior?
[05:38] Priya: runtime supports model variant routing policies and automated fallback to compatible quantized or smaller models. you can configure strictness: strict pinning (no fallback) or permissive (auto fallback). we also expose per-route latency budgets so the router can choose lower-latency options first.
[05:55] Sofia: can we run benchmarks — we want to test a 2k token prompt workload with a 50 qps steady state and occasional spikes to 200 qps. what would be the approach?
[06:03] Priya: our recommended approach:
- Stage 1: small synthetic benchmark in your VPC with PrivateLink to measure raw network RTT and TLS handshake overhead.
- Stage 2: run KV cache warmup with a realistic prefix dataset; capture cache hit ratios.
- Stage 3: run throughput runs with different batching thresholds to measure latency P50, P95, P99 and token cost.
We can run Stage 1/2 with you and provide a script and an artifact in our benchmarking repo.
[06:30] Jordan: we'll also share a benchmark spreadsheet so you can plug in your numbers and see cost vs latency tradeoffs.
[06:35] Carlos: on the subject of cost — is there a per-endpoint charge for PrivateLink or any hidden fees?
[06:40] Jordan: PrivateLink has AWS ENI costs and data processing per GB; our Dedicated contract covers compute and operations, but AWS charges still apply to your account. we'll include a cost worksheet.
[06:50] Liam: if we use Transit Gateway between accounts, do you recommend that vs PrivateLink?
[06:55] Ethan: Transit Gateway is good at scale when you have many VPCs and need full L3 connectivity; PrivateLink is preferred when you want to present a service endpoint without exposing network routing and to keep data plane traffic out of public internet. Transit Gateway can add latency and egress complexity and is more expensive.
[07:12] Meera: any gotchas with mTLS across PrivateLink? we need mutual TLS and client cert rotation.
[07:18] Priya: PrivateLink works with mTLS; you'll need to ensure your certs are trusted and rotation handled on your side. we can support mutual auth and provide CA pinning guidance. cert rotation can be automated with a webhook we provide.
[07:31] Jordan: quick demo of a sample architecture (shared screen) — high level diagram: customer VPC -> interface endpoints (one per AZ) -> NLB in provider VPC -> redwood inference nodes in private subnets. control plane communicates back over a management plane with encrypted channels.
[07:48] Carlos: would you prefer us to expose internal services via interface endpoints or should we peer?
[07:53] Ethan: interface endpoints for service exposure are simpler and give better isolation; peering is more flexible for full mesh but increases blast radius and routing complexity. given your multi-account setup and IP scarcity, PrivateLink usually fits better.
[08:10] Sofia: can we avoid public IPs on the redwood nodes entirely?
[08:13] Priya: yes — nodes can have only private IPs, use interface endpoints or peered connectivity, and egress can be controlled via NAT in your account if needed.
[08:22] Liam: i want to dig into the runtime implications: when kv cache is warm and you use a quantized model, what kind of P95 for token latency are you seeing on GPU-backed instances?
[08:30] Priya: for a mid-sized open model on a modern GPU with kv cache warm and small batch sizes, P50 token latency can be ~6-12 ms, P95 ~18-30 ms. quantization to 8-bit can shave a few ms; 4-bit more so but with risk of slight output degradation. for very low latency use-cases we also offer CPU offload or fp16 kernels tuned to the hardware. these are empirical numbers — we should run your exact model and prompt to be precise.
[09:02] Carlos: are there differences in latency between PrivateLink and a direct peering path?
[09:07] Ethan: peering could be slightly lower latency (bypass NLB), but difference is usually <5 ms. PrivateLink gives better security isolation and simpler cross-account management which often outweighs the tiny delta.
[09:20] Meera: from a compliance standpoint we need audit logs for inference queries. can logs include request ids but not full prompt text?
[09:28] Jordan: yes — we support redaction policies and can store hashes or metadata rather than plain prompts. customer-managed log sink recommended for full control.
[09:36] Sofia: what's the recommended subnet sizing for the nodes? you mentioned /28 per endpoint — what about nodes for inference autoscaling?
[09:44] Ethan: for autoscaling GPU nodes we recommend separate private subnets with a larger block — /22 or /23 depending on autoscale target. keep endpoints and nodes in separate subnets for isolation.
[09:58] Carlos: are there any SDK-level changes we should make — like connection timeouts or header sizes?
[10:03] Priya: we recommend persistent connections (keep-alive), HTTP/2, a client-side retry policy with jitter, and a generous idle timeout for long running streaming responses. also increase file descriptor and ulimit on proxies if you expect high concurrency.
[10:20] Liam: about batching — will you honor per-request latency hints? can we mark some requests as low-latency and bypass batching?
[10:27] Priya: yes — our API supports per-request priority hints and route-level latency SLOs. low-priority requests can be batched aggressively; high-priority requests are routed through the fast-path. we can show SDK examples.
[10:40] Carlos: any special networking for on-prem? we have colo with a transit switch.
[10:45] Jordan: for on-prem we support VPN or Direct Connect style links; you can run redwood nodes in your colo and connect the control plane over a management tunnel. the same principles apply: private IPs, DNS forwarding, and we recommend a small proxy/edge cluster to handle TLS termination and connection pooling.
[11:02] Sofia: can you demo the config for Route 53 resolver rules?
[11:05] Priya: yes — we have a short snippet in the doc. (points to link) https://redwood.inference/docs/private-vpc#route-53-resolver-rules
[11:14] Meera: also want SSO/SAML integration for console access and RBAC for team members.
[11:18] Jordan: we support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC for routes and models. we'll share our security pack and support a compliance call with our security team.
[11:30] Carlos: ok last bit — how do you handle software updates and kernel patches on nodes inside our VPC? we need maintenance windows.
[11:36] Ethan: we support scheduled maintenance windows; updates are rolled with canaries and you control the release window. for critical security patches we chat with your team and can trigger an immediate patch but normally it's scheduled.
[11:50] Jordan: quick recap:
- PrivateLink is preferred given your multi-account setup and IP constraints, with ~2 ms typical overhead.
- Nodes can be private only, use KG-managed telemetry or customer-managed sinks, and support CMK/HSM.
- Runtime tradeoffs: KV cache drastically reduces repeated compute after warmup; batching controls throughput vs latency; quantization reduces cost but needs evals.
- Next steps: we'll share network diagram, benchmark script, cost worksheet, and schedule the benchmark run.
[12:10] Carlos: sounds good. can you send the setup checklist and a list of required IAM roles?
[12:15] Jordan: yes — action items noted. i'll send the checklist and doc links after the call.
[12:22] Sofia: thanks everyone, looking forward to the benchmark.
[12:25] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with dates.
